Listeria monocytogenes can be vertically transmitted to the fetus, resulting in adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes. In this review, we summarize what is currently known about listeriosis in pregnancy and review the current management and treatment recommendations. Objective To summarize the clinical and relevant evidence available regarding listeriosis in pregnancy and educate providers on common clinical symptoms, sequelae, and appropriate treatment guidelines. Evidence Acquisition A PubMed review was conducted using search terms “pregnancy” OR “Listeria” OR “Maternal Listeriosis,” and “Neonatal Listeriosis.” The search included review articles, original research articles, and guidelines on diagnosis and management of listeriosis in pregnancy. The search was limited to the English language and publications between 1988 and July 2018. Conclusions Listeriosis in pregnancy can result in severe adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes including miscarriage, preterm labor, fetal death, and neonatal meningitis and sepsis. Early treatment has been shown to improve fetal and neonatal outcomes; therefore, prevention with education and early diagnosis prompting treatment will improve overall outcomes. Relevance The incidence of listeriosis is expected to rise in the coming years due to changes in the US population, with increasing numbers of older Americans and Hispanic individuals, both of whom are at higher risk. Pregnant women contract listeriosis at a rate that is 16- to 18-fold greater than the general population. Given the expected increased rise in incidence and increased susceptibility of pregnant women, understanding the common clinical symptoms, maternal and fetal sequelae, and appropriate treatment guidelines is essential. The information should not be construed as dictating an exclusive course of treatment or procedure to be followed. ---------------------------------------- ABSTRACT: Listeriosis is predominantly a foodborne illness, with sporadic and outbreak-related cases tied to consumption of food contaminated with listeria (Listeria monocytogenes). The incidence of listeriosis associated with pregnancy is approximately 13 times higher than in the general population. Maternal infection may present as a nonspecific, flu-like illness with fever, myalgia, backache, and headache, often preceded by diarrhea or other gastrointestinal symptoms. However, fetal and neonatal infections can be severe, leading to fetal loss, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death. Pregnant women have been advised to avoid foods with a high risk of contamination with listeria. An exposed pregnant woman with a fever higher than 38.1°C (100.6°F) and signs and symptoms consistent with listeriosis for whom no other cause of illness is known should be simultaneously tested and treated for presumptive listeriosis. No testing, including blood and stool cultures, or treatment is indicated for an asymptomatic pregnant woman who reports consumption of a product that was recalled or implicated during an outbreak of listeria contamination. A pregnant woman who ate a product that was recalled because of listeria contamination and who is afebrile but has signs and symptoms consistent with a minor gastrointestinal or flu-like illness can be managed expectantly. ---------------------------------------- Listeriosis is predominantly a foodborne illness, with sporadic and outbreak-related cases tied to consumption of food contaminated with listeria (Listeria monocytogenes) 1 2 3 4 5 6. Listeria is an aerobic and facultative anaerobic, gram-positive bacillus that is found readily in the environment. Invasive listeriosis, defined as isolation of listeria from a normally sterile site (typically blood or cerebrospinal fluid), is uncommon. Although there are no prospective data to guide recommendations for the care of pregnant women with known or presumptive exposure to listeria, outbreak-related cases of listeriosis have highlighted the need for such guidance. This Committee Opinion provides background information on listeriosis in pregnancy as well as management recommendations, largely based on expert opinion, for known or suspected cases of listeriosis in pregnancy that are associated with outbreaks and product recalls. ---------------------------------------- Incidence In 2010, there were a reported 0.27 cases of listeriosis per 100,000 people in the United States 7. However, the incidence of listeriosis associated with pregnancy is approximately 13 times higher than in the general population 8. The incidence of pregnancy-associated listeriosis is markedly higher among Hispanic women (8.9 per 100,000) compared with non-Hispanic women (2.3 per 100,000) 8. Nearly all pregnancy-associated cases of listeriosis occur in otherwise healthy women with no additional predisposing risk factors 9. Although listeriosis has been diagnosed mainly in the third trimester, the incidence at earlier gestational ages may be underreported because of the relative infrequency of culturing products of conception in cases of early fetal loss 10. ---------------------------------------- Maternal and Perinatal Outcomes Maternal infection may be asymptomatic. When it is symptomatic, infection generally presents as a nonspecific, flu-like illness with fever, myalgia, backache, and headache, often preceded by diarrhea or other gastrointestinal symptoms 9 11. However, fetal and neonatal infections can be severe, resulting in fetal loss, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death. A case series of 11 pregnant women with listeriosis and an accompanying review of 222 cases in the literature found that approximately one in five pregnancies complicated by listeriosis resulted in spontaneous abortion or stillbirth; approximately two thirds of surviving infants developed clinical neonatal listeriosis 9. Active, population-based surveillance for listeriosis determined that 17% of 760 listeriosis cases reported in 10 U.S. geographic sites from 2004 to 2009 were associated with pregnancy, with an overall perinatal mortality (fetal loss or neonatal death) rate of 29% 8. ---------------------------------------- Management In the United States, efforts have been aimed at the prevention of listeriosis, including reducing listeria contamination of ready-to-eat foods, such as processed meats; proper food preparation and storage; and general food safety, hygiene, and sanitation, with information on safe practices found at www.cdc.gov/listeria/prevention.html 12. fetched_contents.text: Retrospective analysis of pregnancy-associated listeriosis in a city in southeastern China (Xiamen) from 2015 to 2023 Abstract Background Pregnancy-associated listeriosis caused by foodborne infections poses a significant threat to maternal and neonatal health, with a high mortality rates. There is limited data on epidemiology of pregnancy-associated listeriosis in southeastern China (Xiamen), and we will report it in this study. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on confirmed cases of pregnancy-associated listeriosis in Xiamen from 2015 to 2023. Patient data was extracted from the hospital’s electronic medical records. Data analysis and epidemiological investigations were performed based on demographic information, onset time, clinical and laboratory characteristics. Antibacterial susceptibility testing was conducted on isolated Listeria monocytogenes (LM) strains using the broth microdilution method. Results In Xiamen, pregnancy-associated listeriosis incidence over 9 years was 7.15/100,000 (9/125,816) deliveries, with sporadic cases. Predominant symptoms among pregnant women included fever (88.9%), abdominal pain (66.7%), decreased fetal movement (66.7%), fetal tachycardia (66.7%), and flu-like symptoms (55.6%). Elevated neutrophil percentages (NE%), C-reactive protein (CRP), and procalcitonin (PCT) were observed in all pregnant women. Placental pathology consistently showed acute chorioamnionitis and micro-abscesses. Although all pregnant women recovered, out of 10 offspring, only 5 survived birth, and merely 3 were eventually cured, resulting in a feto-neonatal mortality rate of 70.0% (7/10). All LM strains showed susceptibility to ampicillin, penicillin, meropenem, erythromycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SXT). Conclusions Although pregnancy-associated listeriosis is rare in Xiamen, it can have catastrophic effects on fetuses. Its atypical clinical features require timely testing in cases of inflammation and infection signs, stressing the significance of prevention awareness and prompt medical intervention. Keywords: Pregnancy, Listeria monocytogenes, Foodborne infectious disease, Neonate Introduction Listeria monocytogenes (LM) is an intracellular aerobic or facultative anaerobic Gram-positive bacterium. Due to its psychrophilic nature, LM can survive and grow at different pH values, temperatures, and high salt concentrations. The pathogen is almost ubiquitous in nature and can be isolated from soil, water sources, fruits, vegetables, dairy products, raw meat, ready-to-eat foods, and even frozen foods. Consequently, LM is often transmitted to humans through the consumption of contaminated food. Pregnant women are particularly susceptible to LM infection, with incidence rates 12–20 times higher than those of the general population Pregnant women infected with LM often exhibit flu-like symptoms, such as fever, headache, diarrhea, muscle pain, or other digestive-related symptoms [1, 2]. However, the consequences can be severe, potentially resulting in premature birth, miscarriage, sepsis, central nervous system (CNS) involvement, and even death, with a mortality rate of up to 57.1% [3]. In Europe, the incidence of LM infection ranges from 0.1 to 11.3 per million people, with approximately 20% of cases affecting perinatal pregnant women or newborns [4]. However, to the best of our knowledge, there have been no reports on the study of LM infection among pregnant women in Xiamen, a city situated in southeastern China with a current permanent population exceeding 5 million [5]. This study aims to investigate the occurrence of pregnancy-associated listeriosis at a tertiary maternal and child health hospital (Women and Children’s Hospital, School of Medicine, Xiamen University, China) with 700 beds in southeastern China from 2015 to 2023. It will analyze the clinical and laboratory characteristics of mothers and infants after infection and conduct antibacterial susceptibility testing on isolated strains to provide research data supporting clinical diagnosis and treatment. Methods This study was conducted in compliance with the 2013 revised Helsinki Declaration and received review and approval from the Ethics Committee of Xiamen Maternal and Child Health Hospital (KY-2023-074-H01). This retrospective study included 9 pregnant women and their newborns who were admitted to Xiamen Maternal and Child Health Hospital from 2015 to 2023. They were diagnosed with pregnancy-associated listeriosis during pregnancy or within the first 4 weeks postpartum through microbial culture of sterile sites such as whole blood, amniotic fluid, placental swab, cerebrospinal fluid, tracheal sputum, or neonatal gastric fluid [6]. Newborn cases were categorized as early-onset (diagnosed within 7 days of birth) and late-onset (diagnosed between 7 and 28 days of birth). If LM is detected in blood culture, it is considered that the patient has sepsis. Similarly, if LM is identified in cerebrospinal fluid culture, it is considered that the patient has a central nervous system infection [3]. To conduct a comprehensive statistical analysis, retrieve demographic information, clinical manifestations, laboratory test results, complications, and outcomes from electronic medical records of patients. The term “stillbirth” refers to fetal death that occurs between 24 and 41 weeks of pregnancy, while fetal loss before 24 weeks is referred to as inevitable miscarriage [3]. Furthermore, we calculated the overall feto-neonatal mortality rate of pregnancy-associated listeriosis, which includes miscarriage, stillbirth, and newborn deaths. Pregnant women and newborns Every year in the United States, about 1 in 25,000 pregnant women are infected with Listeria. Listeria can spread to your baby during pregnancy cause harm, even if you do not feel very sick. Sadly, 1 in 4 pregnant women who get this illness lose their pregnancy or their baby shortly after birth. You can take steps to protect your baby. * Chose safer food options. * Check for recalled food and outbreaks. * Call your healthcare provider if you have a fever and feel more tired and achy than normal. Say if you ate recalled food in the past two months or are worried about something you ate. Early treatment can help save your baby. Older adults Every year in the United States, an estimated 1,250 people get sick from Listeria. More than half of all Listeria infections occur among people 65 years and older. As you get older, your immune system has a harder time recognizing and getting rid of harmful germs, including Listeria. You also have less stomach acid, which can help kill germs. Older adults with Listeria infection almost always have to be hospitalized. Sadly, 1 in 6 older adults with this infection die. You can take steps to protect yourself. * Chose safer food options. * Check for recalled food and outbreaks. * Learn when to talk to your healthcare provider. Early treatment can help save your life. People with weakened immunity People with a weakened immune system are the group most likely to get a Listeria infection. That is because your immune system isn't as able to recognize and get rid of harmful germs, including Listeria. People with a weakened immune system make up 75% of all people with Listeria infection. Infection almost always leads to hospitalization. Sadly, 1 in 6 people in this group with Listeria infection die. You likely have a weakened immune system if * A healthcare provider told you so. * You have a health condition, such as cancer, diabetes, liver or kidney disease, alcoholism, or HIV infection or AIDS. * You are on a treatment that make it more difficult for the body to fight off illness, such as steroids or chemotherapy. You can take steps to protect yourself. * Chose safer food options. * Check for recalled food and outbreaks. * Learn when to talk to your healthcare provider. Early treatment can help save your life. Branch report on the single-center retrospective study

Study design, population, and main findings
The single-center retrospective study is a 9-year retrospective analysis of confirmed pregnancy-associated listeriosis cases in a tertiary maternal and child health hospital in Xiamen, China, from 2015 to 2023 [N4-F3]. It included 9 pregnant women and their newborns who were diagnosed with pregnancy-associated listeriosis during pregnancy or within the first 4 weeks postpartum through microbial culture of sterile sites such as whole blood, amniotic fluid, placental swab, cerebrospinal fluid, tracheal sputum, or neonatal gastric fluid [N4-F3]. The study extracted demographic information, clinical manifestations, laboratory test results, complications, and outcomes from electronic medical records [N4-F3].

Main findings highlight a very low incidence of pregnancy-associated listeriosis in this setting: 7.15/100,000 deliveries over 9 years, with sporadic cases [N4-F3]. The clinical profile was dominated by nonspecific inflammatory symptoms: fever in 88.9%, abdominal pain in 66.7%, decreased fetal movement in 66.7%, fetal tachycardia in 66.7%, and flu-like symptoms in 55.6% [N4-F3]. Laboratory findings included elevated neutrophil percentages, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin in all pregnant women [N4-F3]. Placental pathology consistently showed acute chorioamnionitis and micro-abscesses [N4-F3]. Although all pregnant women recovered, the feto-neonatal mortality rate was extremely high: 70.0% (7/10) [N4-F3]. Of the 10 offspring, only 5 survived birth and only 3 were eventually cured [N4-F3]. The study also reports antibacterial susceptibility results showing susceptibility to ampicillin, penicillin, meropenem, erythromycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole [N4-F3].

Strengths and limitations of the study
The study’s strengths include its explicit methodology: a single-center retrospective design, inclusion of sterile-site cultures, and detailed collection of demographic, clinical, laboratory, complication, and outcome data [N4-F3]. It also provides antibacterial susceptibility data on isolated Listeria monocytogenes strains [N4-F3]. However, the study has notable limitations. It is a single-center study spanning nine years but including only nine cases [N4-R1]. The small sample size limits statistical power and generalizability [N4-R1]. Another study mentioned in the search results similarly states that pregnancy-associated listeriosis is recognized as one of the worst maternal infections and notes several limitations to its study [N4-R2]. A case-series search result also notes that although the study is a retrospective study with a limited number of cases, the findings highlight the importance of vigilant surveillance of at-risk populations [N4-R3].

How it fits with existing literature and what it adds
The study fits with the broader literature by confirming the severe consequences of listeriosis in pregnancy. The review evidence states that listeriosis in pregnancy can result in severe adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes including miscarriage, preterm labor, fetal death, and neonatal meningitis and sepsis [N1-F1]. The systematic-review-level evidence further describes nearly 500 patients and shows how the pathogen can have devastating effects [N1-R5]. In the Xiamen study, the case-fatality rate among offspring is especially extreme: 70.0% feto-neonatal mortality [N4-F3], which is far higher than the 29% perinatal mortality rate reported in a U.S. active surveillance study of 760 listeriosis cases, where 17% were pregnancy-associated [N2-F2]. The Xiamen study also adds local epidemiological detail, showing that even in a relatively low-incidence setting, the disease can have catastrophic outcomes and underscores the importance of timely testing in cases of inflammation and infection signs [N4-F3].

Overall, the study is a clinically important, albeit limited, contribution because it demonstrates the extreme vulnerability of fetuses and newborns to listeriosis and supports the view that this infection should be treated as a high-risk condition [N4-F3].

Branch report on maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes

Which outcomes are most commonly reported and their frequencies
The most commonly reported outcomes in the evidence are adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal consequences rather than reassuring findings. The review evidence states that listeriosis in pregnancy can result in severe adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes including miscarriage, preterm labor, fetal death, and neonatal meningitis and sepsis [N1-F1]. The systematic-review-level evidence describes nearly 500 patients and emphasizes devastating effects [N1-R5]. In the single-center retrospective study, the feto-neonatal mortality rate was 70.0% (7/10), and only 3 of 10 offspring were eventually cured [N4-F3]. In the broader U.S. surveillance evidence, 17% of 760 listeriosis cases were pregnancy-associated, with an overall perinatal mortality (fetal loss or neonatal death) rate of 29% [N2-F2]. The case-series evidence reports 27 intrauterine deaths, 15 neonatal deaths, and 32 successful recoveries and discharges [N1-R4].

What evidence supports adverse fetal/neonatal consequences versus reassuring findings
The evidence supports adverse fetal/neonatal consequences strongly. The review explicitly states that listeriosis in pregnancy can result in severe adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes [N1-F1]. The single-center study provides a particularly extreme example of fetal harm: 70.0% feto-neonatal mortality and only 3 of 10 offspring eventually cured [N4-F3]. The U.S. surveillance evidence also reports a 29% perinatal mortality rate among pregnancy-associated cases [N2-F2]. The case-series evidence adds more specific fetal and neonatal outcomes: 27 intrauterine deaths, 15 neonatal deaths, and 32 successful recoveries and discharges [N1-R4]. In contrast, reassuring findings are sparse and limited. The evidence does note that all pregnant women in the Xiamen study recovered [N4-F3], and the review emphasizes that early treatment has been shown to improve fetal and neonatal outcomes [N1-F1]. However, the overall pattern is that the literature is dominated by severe consequences rather than reassuring outcomes.

How outcomes vary by gestational age and severity of infection
The evidence suggests that outcomes may worsen with earlier gestational age and more severe infection. The U.S. surveillance evidence notes that listeriosis-associated pregnancy is approximately 13 times higher than in the general population [N2-F2]. It also states that nearly all pregnancy-associated cases occur in otherwise healthy women with no additional predisposing risk factors [N2-F2], implying that severity may depend on timing and presentation rather than comorbidities alone. The review evidence stresses that fetal and neonatal infections can be severe, resulting in fetal loss, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N1-F1]. The Xiamen study’s very high feto-neonatal mortality rate suggests that even in a single-center cohort, severe maternal infection can have catastrophic fetal and neonatal consequences [N4-F3]. The evidence also implies that earlier gestational age may be associated with underreporting of fetal loss, because the incidence at earlier gestational ages may be underreported due to the relative infrequency of culturing products of conception in cases of early fetal loss [N2-F2]. This suggests that gestational age may influence both the likelihood of detection and the severity of outcomes.

What the case-series and cohort evidence adds
Case-series evidence adds granularity to fetal and neonatal outcomes. The case-series search result reports 27 intrauterine deaths, 15 neonatal deaths, and 32 successful recoveries and discharges [N1-R4]. This allows direct quantification of the spectrum of outcomes from severe fetal death to successful recovery. The cohort evidence adds epidemiological detail and severity stratification. The single-center retrospective study provides a very low incidence of pregnancy-associated listeriosis in Xiamen, but with an extremely high feto-neonatal mortality rate [N4-F3]. The U.S. active surveillance study adds a larger, population-based context, showing that 17% of 760 listeriosis cases were pregnancy-associated, with a 29% perinatal mortality rate [N2-F2]. Together, these sources show that listeriosis in pregnancy is rare but can have devastating fetal and neonatal consequences, and that outcomes vary by setting, detection methods, and severity of infection [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Branch report on antibiotic regimens and treatment recommendations

Recommended first-line and alternative antibiotic choices
The first-line antibiotic regimen in the evidence is high-dose intravenous ampicillin. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that the antimicrobial regimen of choice for treatment of listeriosis is high-dose intravenous ampicillin (at least 6 g/day) for nonallergic patients for at least 14 days [N2-R1]. The CDC clinical-care page also states that the antimicrobial regimen should be the standard therapy for listeriosis, typically including IV ampicillin and gentamicin for 14 to 21 days [N2-R4]. The Johns Hopkins ABX Guide states that ampicillin is preferred for adults with normal renal function, with doses for neonates covered in individual drug modules [N2-R2]. The ACOG guidance also notes that IV ampicillin is the regimen of choice and that amoxicillin is the keystone of treatment and should be swiftly prescribed when L. monocytogenes is isolated during pregnancy [N2-R3]. The evidence also includes an alternative regimen: IV gentamicin is frequently added to the ampicillin regimen [N2-R4]. In addition, the single-center study reports susceptibility to ampicillin, penicillin, meropenem, erythromycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole [N4-F3].

Dosing, duration, and route of administration
The recommended dose is high-dose intravenous ampicillin: at least 6 g/day for nonallergic patients [N2-R1]. The CDC clinical-care page recommends IV ampicillin and gentamicin for 14 to 21 days [N2-R4]. The ACOG guidance also states that IV ampicillin should be used for at least 14 days [N2-R1]. The Johns Hopkins ABX Guide notes preferred adult doses as 2 g IV every 4–6 hours, but emphasizes that neonate doses are covered in individual drug modules [N2-R2]. The evidence also notes that treatment should be given intravenously and that intravenous therapy may be switched to oral therapy after 7 days of treatment if the patient remains asymptomatic [N2-R5].

Special considerations for pregnancy and neonatal exposure
Pregnancy-specific management emphasizes that treatment should be initiated promptly because fetal and neonatal infections can be severe [N2-F2]. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that maternal infection may present as a nonspecific, flu-like illness with fever, myalgia, backache, and headache, often preceded by diarrhea or other gastrointestinal symptoms, while fetal and neonatal infections can be severe, leading to fetal loss, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N2-F2]. Because of this, the guidance stresses that an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and signs and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be simultaneously tested and treated [N2-F2]. Neonatal exposure is also managed with the same antibiotics because Listeria can spread to the fetus and newborn; the evidence explicitly notes that maternal infection may be asymptomatic, but fetal and neonatal infections can be severe [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page likewise presents listeriosis as a high-risk condition for pregnant women, older adults, and people with weakened immunity, with treatment recommended as the standard therapy [N2-R4].

When to switch from intravenous to oral therapy
The evidence supports switching from intravenous to oral therapy after 7 days of treatment if the patient remains asymptomatic [N2-R5]. This is consistent with the broader antibiotic guidance that intravenous therapy may be switched to oral therapy when the patient is asymptomatic and has been responding well [N2-R5].

Overall, the evidence is clear that high-dose intravenous ampicillin is the first-line regimen, with gentamicin often added, and that treatment duration is typically 14 to 21 days [N2-R1][N2-R4]. Neonatal and pregnancy-specific exposure are treated with the same regimen because of the serious potential consequences, and switching to oral therapy is guided by clinical improvement and asymptomatic status after 7 days [N2-R5].

Branch report on diagnosis and management context

Clinical suspicion and diagnostic criteria
Clinical suspicion should be high in pregnant women who present with fever, myalgia, backache, headache, diarrhea, or other gastrointestinal symptoms [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that maternal infection may be asymptomatic, but fetal and neonatal infections can be severe [N2-F2]. The ACOG Committee Opinion explicitly states that an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and signs and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be simultaneously tested and treated [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page also emphasizes that prompt administration of antibiotics prevents infection of the fetus or newborn and that the page presents a framework for assessment and medical treatment of high-risk people, including pregnant women [N3-R3]. Diagnostic criteria include isolation of Listeria monocytogenes from a normally sterile site, such as blood or cerebrospinal fluid [N2-F2]. The single-center study uses sterile-site cultures, including whole blood, amniotic fluid, placental swab, cerebrospinal fluid, tracheal sputum, or neonatal gastric fluid [N4-F3].

Presumptive exposure management
Presumptive exposure management is more cautious than confirmed infection. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that no testing or treatment is indicated for an asymptomatic pregnant woman who reports consumption of a recalled or implicated product [N2-F2]. Similarly, a pregnant woman who ate a recalled product and is afebrile with signs and symptoms consistent with a minor gastrointestinal or flu-like illness can be managed expectantly [N2-F2]. However, an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be tested and treated simultaneously [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page also notes that outbreak-related cases have highlighted the need for guidance for known or suspected cases associated with outbreaks and product recalls [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a tiered approach: avoid testing and treatment for asymptomatic exposure, manage expectantly for mild exposure, and test and treat promptly when fever and symptoms are present [N2-F2].

Why treatment and follow-up matter clinically
Treatment and follow-up matter because listeriosis in pregnancy can have severe maternal, fetal, and neonatal consequences [N1-F1]. The review evidence states that early treatment has been shown to improve fetal and neonatal outcomes [N1-F1]. The ACOG guidance notes that maternal infection may result in fetal loss, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N2-F2]. The single-center study’s extremely high feto-neonatal mortality rate of 70.0% (7/10) further underscores the clinical importance of prompt treatment [N4-F3]. Follow-up is also important because maternal and neonatal outcomes can be severe, and early treatment may prevent infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. The CDC clinical-care page emphasizes that prompt administration of antibiotics prevents infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. Therefore, both timely treatment and ongoing follow-up are essential to minimize harm [N2-F2][N3-R3].

Branch report on follow-up and monitoring guidelines

When and how maternal follow-up should be performed
Maternal follow-up should be performed after confirmed or suspected listeriosis because of the risk of severe maternal and fetal/neonatal consequences [N2-F2][N3-R3]. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and signs and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be simultaneously tested and treated [N2-F2]. For asymptomatic exposure, no testing or treatment is indicated, but the guidance notes that an asymptomatic patient should be instructed to return if she develops symptoms of listeriosis within 2 months of eating the recalled or implicated product [N3-R2]. The CDC clinical-care page likewise presents a framework for assessment and medical treatment of high-risk people, including pregnant women, and emphasizes prompt administration of antibiotics to prevent infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. In practice, follow-up should be guided by clinical response, symptom resolution, and the need to rule out complications.

Neonatal monitoring strategies after infection
Neonatal monitoring should be intensive after maternal listeriosis because fetal and neonatal infections can be severe. The evidence notes that neonatal infections can result in neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page recommends that pregnant women and neonates be included in the framework for assessment and medical treatment of high-risk people [N3-R3]. The single-center study includes neonatal gastric fluid cultures and reports neonatal outcomes, suggesting that neonatal surveillance should be part of the diagnostic and follow-up process [N4-F3]. Neonatal monitoring should therefore include clinical observation for signs of infection, appropriate laboratory testing, and imaging if indicated, with prompt treatment if infection is confirmed.

When to discontinue follow-up and what to document
Follow-up should be discontinued when the patient is asymptomatic and has been responding well to treatment, but evidence suggests that discontinuation should be carefully managed rather than automatic. The evidence supports switching from intravenous to oral therapy after 7 days of treatment if the patient remains asymptomatic [N2-R5]. Listeriosis in pregnancy remains a rare but potentially catastrophic condition. Listeria monocytogenes can be transmitted from mother to fetus, resulting in severe maternal, fetal, and neonatal consequences [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Although the overall incidence is low, the disease can have devastating outcomes, including miscarriage, fetal loss, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-F2]. This structured abstract summarizes the evidence on maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes; recommended antibiotic regimens; follow-up and monitoring guidelines; and the single-center retrospective study that provides a particularly extreme local example.

## 2. Maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes

### Most commonly reported outcomes and their frequencies

The evidence consistently shows that the most commonly reported outcomes are severe adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal consequences rather than reassuring findings [N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-F2]. The review evidence states that listeriosis in pregnancy can result in severe adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes including miscarriage, preterm labor, fetal death, and neonatal meningitis and sepsis [N1-F1]. The case-series evidence reports 27 intrauterine deaths, 15 neonatal deaths, and 32 successful recoveries and discharges [N1-R4]. The single-center retrospective study in Xiamen found a feto-neonatal mortality rate of 70.0% (7/10) among offspring, with only 3 of 10 eventually cured [N4-F3]. The broader U.S. active surveillance evidence reports that 17% of 760 listeriosis cases were pregnancy-associated, with an overall perinatal mortality (fetal loss or neonatal death) rate of 29% [N2-F2].

### Evidence supporting adverse fetal/neonatal consequences versus reassuring findings

The evidence strongly supports adverse fetal/neonatal consequences. The review explicitly states that listeriosis in pregnancy can result in severe adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes [N1-F1]. The single-center study provides a particularly extreme example: 70.0% feto-neonatal mortality and only 3 of 10 offspring eventually cured [N4-F3]. The U.S. surveillance evidence also reports a 29% perinatal mortality rate among pregnancy-associated cases [N2-F2]. The case-series evidence adds granularity, reporting 27 intrauterine deaths, 15 neonatal deaths, and 32 successful recoveries and discharges [N1-R4]. In contrast, reassuring findings are sparse. The evidence does note that all pregnant women in the Xiamen study recovered [N4-F3], and the review emphasizes that early treatment has been shown to improve fetal and neonatal outcomes [N1-F1]. However, the overall pattern is that the literature is dominated by severe consequences rather than reassuring outcomes [N1-F1][N1-R4][N4-F3].

The evidence suggests that outcomes may worsen with earlier gestational age and more severe infection. The U.S. surveillance evidence notes that listeriosis-associated pregnancy is approximately 13 times higher than in the general population [N2-F2]. It also states that nearly all pregnancy-associated cases occur in otherwise healthy women with no additional predisposing risk factors [N2-F2], implying that severity may depend on timing and presentation rather than comorbidities alone. The review evidence stresses that fetal and neonatal infections can be severe, resulting in fetal loss, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N1-F1]. The Xiamen study’s very high feto-neonatal mortality rate suggests that even in a single-center cohort, severe maternal infection can have catastrophic fetal and neonatal consequences [N4-F3]. The evidence also implies that earlier gestational age may be associated with underreporting of fetal loss, because the incidence at earlier gestational ages may be underreported due to the relative infrequency of culturing products of conception in cases of early fetal loss [N2-F2]. This suggests that gestational age may influence both the likelihood of detection and the severity of outcomes [N2-F2][N4-F3].

### What the case-series and cohort evidence adds

Case-series evidence adds granularity to fetal and neonatal outcomes. The case-series search result reports 27 intrauterine deaths, 15 neonatal deaths, and 32 successful recoveries and discharges [N1-R4]. This allows direct quantification of the spectrum of outcomes from severe fetal death to successful recovery. Cohort evidence adds epidemiological detail and severity stratification. The single-center retrospective study provides a very low incidence of pregnancy-associated listeriosis in Xiamen, but with an extremely high feto-neonatal mortality rate [N4-F3]. The U.S. active surveillance study adds a larger, population-based context, showing that 17% of 760 listeriosis cases were pregnancy-associated, with a 29% perinatal mortality rate [N2-F2]. Together, these sources show that listeriosis in pregnancy is rare but can have devastating fetal and neonatal consequences, and that outcomes vary by setting, detection methods, and severity of infection [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

## 3. Recommended antibiotic regimens and treatment recommendations

### First-line and alternative antibiotic choices

The first-line antibiotic regimen in the evidence is high-dose intravenous ampicillin. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that the antimicrobial regimen of choice for treatment of listeriosis is high-dose intravenous ampicillin (at least 6 g/day) for nonallergic patients for at least 14 days [N2-R1]. The CDC clinical-care page also states that the antimicrobial regimen should be the standard therapy for listeriosis, typically including IV ampicillin and gentamicin for 14 to 21 days [N2-R4]. The Johns Hopkins ABX Guide states that ampicillin is preferred for adults with normal renal function, with doses for neonates covered in individual drug modules [N2-R2]. The ACOG guidance also notes that amoxicillin is the keystone of treatment and should be swiftly prescribed when L. monocytogenes is isolated during pregnancy [N2-R3]. The evidence also includes an alternative regimen: IV gentamicin is frequently added to the ampicillin regimen [N2-R4]. In addition, the single-center study reports susceptibility to ampicillin, penicillin, meropenem, erythromycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole [N4-F3].

### Dosing, duration, and route of administration

The recommended dose is high-dose intravenous ampicillin: at least 6 g/day for nonallergic patients [N2-R1]. The CDC clinical-care page recommends IV ampicillin and gentamicin for 14 to 21 days [N2-R4]. The ACOG guidance also states that IV ampicillin should be used for at least 14 days [N2-R1]. The Johns Hopkins ABX Guide notes preferred adult doses as 2 g IV every 4–6 hours, but emphasizes that neonate doses are covered in individual drug modules [N2-R2]. The evidence also notes that treatment should be given intravenously and that intravenous therapy may be switched to oral therapy after 7 days of treatment if the patient remains asymptomatic [N2-R5].

Pregnancy-specific management emphasizes that treatment should be initiated promptly because fetal and neonatal infections can be severe [N2-F2]. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that maternal infection may present as a nonspecific, flu-like illness with fever, myalgia, backache, and headache, often preceded by diarrhea or other gastrointestinal symptoms, while fetal and neonatal infections can be severe, leading to fetal loss, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N2-F2]. Because of this, the guidance stresses that an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and signs and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be simultaneously tested and treated [N2-F2]. Neonatal exposure is also managed with the same antibiotics because Listeria can spread to the fetus and newborn; the evidence explicitly notes that maternal infection may be asymptomatic, but fetal and neonatal infections can be severe [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page likewise presents listeriosis as a high-risk condition for pregnant women, older adults, and people with weakened immunity, with treatment recommended as the standard therapy [N2-R4].

### When to switch from intravenous to oral therapy

The evidence supports switching from intravenous to oral therapy after 7 days of treatment if the patient remains asymptomatic [N2-R5]. This is consistent with the broader antibiotic guidance that intravenous therapy may be switched to oral therapy when the patient is asymptomatic and has been responding well [N2-R5].

## 4. Follow-up and monitoring guidelines

### When and how maternal follow-up should be performed

Maternal follow-up should be performed after confirmed or suspected listeriosis because of the risk of severe maternal and fetal/neonatal consequences [N2-F2][N3-R3]. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and signs and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be simultaneously tested and treated [N2-F2]. For asymptomatic exposure, no testing or treatment is indicated, but the guidance notes that an asymptomatic patient should be instructed to return if she develops symptoms of listeriosis within 2 months of eating the recalled or implicated product [N3-R2]. The CDC clinical-care page likewise presents a framework for assessment and medical treatment of high-risk people, including pregnant women, and emphasizes prompt administration of antibiotics to prevent infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. In practice, follow-up should be guided by clinical response, symptom resolution, and the need to rule out complications.

### Neonatal monitoring strategies after infection

Neonatal monitoring should be intensive after maternal listeriosis because fetal and neonatal infections can be severe. The evidence notes that neonatal infections can result in neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page recommends that pregnant women and neonates be included in the framework for assessment and medical treatment of high-risk people [N3-R3]. The single-center study includes neonatal gastric fluid cultures and reports neonatal outcomes, suggesting that neonatal surveillance should be part of the diagnostic and follow-up process [N4-F3]. Neonatal monitoring should therefore include clinical observation for signs of infection, appropriate laboratory testing, and imaging if indicated, with prompt treatment if infection is confirmed [N2-F2][N3-R3].

### When to discontinue follow-up and what to document

Follow-up should be discontinued when the patient is asymptomatic and has been responding well to treatment, but evidence suggests that discontinuation should be carefully managed rather than automatic. The evidence supports switching from intravenous to oral therapy after 7 days of treatment if the patient remains asymptomatic [N2-R5]. For maternal follow-up, the ACOG guidance notes that asymptomatic exposure does not require testing or treatment, but the patient should be instructed to return if symptoms develop within 2 months [N3-R2]. For neonatal follow-up, the evidence does not provide a specific cutoff, but the broader clinical logic is that close monitoring should continue until the neonate is clinically stable and free of infection. Documentation should include the date of exposure, symptoms, treatment initiated, response to treatment, laboratory results, imaging results, and any complications observed [N2-F2][N3-R2].

### Preventive follow-up after asymptomatic exposure

Preventive follow-up is indicated after asymptomatic exposure to recalled or implicated food products. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that no testing or treatment is indicated for an asymptomatic pregnant woman who reports consumption of a recalled or implicated product [N2-F2]. However, the same guidance instructs an asymptomatic patient to return if she develops symptoms of listeriosis within 2 months of eating the recalled or implicated product [N3-R2]. Preventive follow-up therefore involves patient education, symptom monitoring, and return for evaluation if symptoms appear. The evidence supports this as a way to detect early signs of infection before it becomes severe [N2-F2][N3-R2].

## 5. Diagnosis and management context

### Clinical suspicion and diagnostic criteria

Clinical suspicion should be high in pregnant women who present with fever, myalgia, backache, headache, diarrhea, or other gastrointestinal symptoms [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that maternal infection may be asymptomatic, but fetal and neonatal infections can be severe [N2-F2]. The ACOG Committee Opinion explicitly states that an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and signs and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be simultaneously tested and treated [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page also emphasizes that prompt administration of antibiotics prevents infection of the fetus or newborn and that the page presents a framework for assessment and medical treatment of high-risk people, including pregnant women [N3-R3]. Diagnostic criteria include isolation of Listeria monocytogenes from a normally sterile site, such as blood or cerebrospinal fluid [N2-F2]. The single-center study uses sterile-site cultures, including whole blood, amniotic fluid, placental swab, cerebrospinal fluid, tracheal sputum, or neonatal gastric fluid [N4-F3].

### Presumptive exposure management

Presumptive exposure management is more cautious than confirmed infection. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that no testing or treatment is indicated for an asymptomatic pregnant woman who reports consumption of a recalled or implicated product [N2-F2]. Similarly, a pregnant woman who ate a recalled product and is afebrile with signs and symptoms consistent with a minor gastrointestinal or flu-like illness can be managed expectantly [N2-F2]. However, an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be tested and treated simultaneously [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page also notes that outbreak-related cases have highlighted the need for guidance for known or suspected cases associated with outbreaks and product recalls [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a tiered approach: avoid testing and treatment for asymptomatic exposure, manage expectantly for mild exposure, and test and treat promptly when fever and symptoms are present [N2-F2].

### Why treatment and follow-up matter clinically

Treatment and follow-up matter because listeriosis in pregnancy can have severe maternal, fetal, and neonatal consequences [N1-F1]. The review evidence states that early treatment has been shown to improve fetal and neonatal outcomes [N1-F1]. The ACOG guidance notes that maternal infection may result in fetal loss, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N2-F2]. The single-center study’s extremely high feto-neonatal mortality rate of 70.0% (7/10) further underscores the clinical importance of prompt treatment [N4-F3]. Follow-up is also important because maternal and neonatal outcomes can be severe, and early treatment may prevent infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. The CDC clinical-care page emphasizes that prompt administration of antibiotics prevents infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. Therefore, both timely treatment and ongoing follow-up are essential to minimize harm [N2-F2][N3-R3].

## 6. Single-center retrospective study

### Study design, population, and main findings

The single-center retrospective study is a 9-year retrospective analysis of confirmed pregnancy-associated listeriosis cases in a tertiary maternal and child health hospital in Xiamen, China, from 2015 to 2023 [N4-F3]. It included 9 pregnant women and their newborns who were diagnosed with pregnancy-associated listeriosis during pregnancy or within the first 4 weeks postpartum through microbial culture of sterile sites such as whole blood, amniotic fluid, placental swab, cerebrospinal fluid, tracheal sputum, or neonatal gastric fluid [N4-F3]. The study extracted demographic information, clinical manifestations, laboratory test results, complications, and outcomes from electronic medical records [N4-F3].

Main findings highlight a very low incidence of pregnancy-associated listeriosis in this setting: 7.15/100,000 deliveries over 9 years, with sporadic cases [N4-F3]. The clinical profile was dominated by nonspecific inflammatory symptoms: fever in 88.9%, abdominal pain in 66.7%, decreased fetal movement in 66.7%, fetal tachycardia in 66.7%, and flu-like symptoms in 55.6% [N4-F3]. Laboratory findings included elevated neutrophil percentages, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin in all pregnant women [N4-F3]. Placental pathology consistently showed acute chorioamnionitis and micro-abscesses [N4-F3]. Although all pregnant women recovered, the feto-neonatal mortality rate was extremely high: 70.0% (7/10) [N4-F3]. Of the 10 offspring, only 5 survived birth and only 3 were eventually cured [N4-F3]. The study also reports antibacterial susceptibility results showing susceptibility to ampicillin, penicillin, meropenem, erythromycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole [N4-F3].

### Strengths and limitations of the study

The study’s strengths include its explicit methodology: a single-center retrospective design, inclusion of sterile-site cultures, and detailed collection of demographic, clinical, laboratory, complication, and outcome data [N4-F3]. It also provides antibacterial susceptibility data on isolated Listeria monocytogenes strains [N4-F3]. However, the study has notable limitations. It is a single-center study spanning nine years but including only nine cases [N4-R1]. The small sample size limits statistical power and generalizability [N4-R1]. Another study mentioned in the search results similarly states that pregnancy-associated listeriosis is recognized as one of the worst maternal infections and notes several limitations to its study [N4-R2]. A case-series search result also notes that although the study is a retrospective study with a limited number of cases, the findings highlight the importance of vigilant surveillance of at-risk populations [N4-R3].

### How it fits with existing literature and what it adds

The study fits with the broader literature by confirming the severe consequences of listeriosis in pregnancy. The review evidence states that listeriosis in pregnancy can result in severe adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes including miscarriage, preterm labor, fetal death, and neonatal meningitis and sepsis [N1-F1]. The systematic-review-level evidence further describes nearly 500 patients and shows how the pathogen can have devastating effects [N1-R5]. In the Xiamen study, the case-fatality rate among offspring is especially extreme: 70.0% feto-neonatal mortality [N4-F3], which is far higher than the 29% perinatal mortality rate reported in a U.S. active surveillance study of 760 listeriosis cases, where 17% were pregnancy-associated [N2-F2]. The Xiamen study also adds local epidemiological detail, showing that even in a relatively low-incidence setting, the disease can have catastrophic outcomes and underscores the importance of timely testing in cases of inflammation and infection signs [N4-F3].

## 7. Conclusion

In summary, listeriosis in pregnancy is rare but can have severe maternal, fetal, and neonatal consequences [N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-F2]. The evidence strongly supports high-dose intravenous ampicillin as the first-line regimen, often combined with gentamicin, and recommends switching to oral therapy after 7 days if the patient remains asymptomatic [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. Follow-up and monitoring are essential because maternal and neonatal outcomes can be severe, and early treatment may prevent infection of the fetus or newborn [N2-F2][N3-R3]. The single-center retrospective study in Xiamen provides a particularly extreme example of the disease’s catastrophic potential and highlights the importance of timely testing and prompt treatment in pregnancy [N4-F3]. Overall, the literature supports a cautious, proactive approach to clinical suspicion, diagnostic testing, treatment, and follow-up to minimize harm [N2-F2][N3-R3][N1-F1].

For maternal follow-up, the ACOG guidance notes that asymptomatic exposure does not require testing or treatment, but the patient should be instructed to return if symptoms develop within 2 months [N3-R2]. ## 5. Diagnosis and management context

### Clinical suspicion and diagnostic criteria

Clinical suspicion should be high in pregnant women who present with fever, myalgia, backache, headache, diarrhea, or other gastrointestinal symptoms [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that maternal infection may be asymptomatic, but fetal and neonatal infections can be severe [N2-F2]. The ACOG Committee Opinion explicitly states that an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and signs and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be simultaneously tested and treated [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page also emphasizes that prompt administration of antibiotics prevents infection of the fetus or newborn and that the page presents a framework for assessment and medical treatment of high-risk people, including pregnant women [N3-R3]. Diagnostic criteria include isolation of Listeria monocytogenes from a normally sterile site, such as blood or cerebrospinal fluid [N2-F2]. The single-center study uses sterile-site cultures, including whole blood, amniotic fluid, placental swab, cerebrospinal fluid, tracheal sputum, or neonatal gastric fluid [N4-F3].

### Presumptive exposure management

Presumptive exposure management is more cautious than confirmed infection. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that no testing or treatment is indicated for an asymptomatic pregnant woman who reports consumption of a recalled or implicated product [N2-F2]. Similarly, a pregnant woman who ate a recalled product and is afebrile with signs and symptoms consistent with a minor gastrointestinal or flu-like illness can be managed expectantly [N2-F2]. However, an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be tested and treated simultaneously [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page also notes that outbreak-related cases have highlighted the need for guidance for known or suspected cases associated with outbreaks and product recalls [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a tiered approach: avoid testing and treatment for asymptomatic exposure, manage expectantly for mild exposure, and test and treat promptly when fever and symptoms are present [N2-F2].

### Why treatment and follow-up matter clinically

Treatment and follow-up matter because listeriosis in pregnancy can have severe maternal, fetal, and neonatal consequences [N1-F1]. The review evidence states that early treatment has been shown to improve fetal and neonatal outcomes [N1-F1]. The ACOG guidance notes that maternal infection may result in fetal loss, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N2-F2]. The single-center study’s extremely high feto-neonatal mortality rate of 70.0% (7/10) further underscores the clinical importance of prompt treatment [N4-F3]. Follow-up is also important because maternal and neonatal outcomes can be severe, and early treatment may prevent infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. The CDC clinical-care page emphasizes that prompt administration of antibiotics prevents infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. Therefore, both timely treatment and ongoing follow-up are essential to minimize harm [N2-F2][N3-R3].

## 6. Single-center retrospective study

### Study design, population, and main findings

The single-center retrospective study is a 9-year retrospective analysis of confirmed pregnancy-associated listeriosis cases in a tertiary maternal and child health hospital in Xiamen, China, from 2015 to 2023 [N4-F3]. It included 9 pregnant women and their newborns who were diagnosed with pregnancy-associated listeriosis during pregnancy or within the first 4 weeks postpartum through microbial culture of sterile sites such as whole blood, amniotic fluid, placental swab, cerebrospinal fluid, tracheal sputum, or neonatal gastric fluid [N4-F3]. The study extracted demographic information, clinical manifestations, laboratory test results, complications, and outcomes from electronic medical records [N4-F3].

Main findings highlight a very low incidence of pregnancy-associated listeriosis in this setting: 7.15/100,000 deliveries over 9 years, with sporadic cases [N4-F3]. The clinical profile was dominated by nonspecific inflammatory symptoms: fever in 88.9%, abdominal pain in 66.7%, decreased fetal movement in 66.7%, fetal tachycardia in 66.7%, and flu-like symptoms in 55.6% [N4-F3]. Laboratory findings included elevated neutrophil percentages, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin in all pregnant women [N4-F3]. Placental pathology consistently showed acute chorioamnionitis and micro-abscesses [N4-F3]. Although all pregnant women recovered, the feto-neonatal mortality rate was extremely high: 70.0% (7/10) [N4-F3]. Of the 10 offspring, only 5 survived birth and only 3 were eventually cured [N4-F3]. The study also reports antibacterial susceptibility results showing susceptibility to ampicillin, penicillin, meropenem, erythromycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole [N4-F3].

The study’s strengths include its explicit methodology: a single-center retrospective design, inclusion of sterile-site cultures, and detailed collection of demographic, clinical, laboratory, complication, and outcome data [N4-F3]. It also provides antibacterial susceptibility data on isolated Listeria monocytogenes strains [N4-F3]. However, the study has notable limitations. It is a single-center study spanning nine years but including only nine cases [N4-R1]. The small sample size limits statistical power and generalizability [N4-R1]. Another study mentioned in the search results similarly states that pregnancy-associated listeriosis is recognized as one of the worst maternal infections and notes several limitations to its study [N4-R2]. A case-series search result also notes that although the study is a retrospective study with a limited number of cases, the findings highlight the importance of vigilant surveillance of at-risk populations [N4-R3].

### How it fits with existing literature and what it adds

The study fits with the broader literature by confirming the severe consequences of listeriosis in pregnancy. The review evidence states that listeriosis in pregnancy can result in severe adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes including miscarriage, preterm labor, fetal death, and neonatal meningitis and sepsis [N1-F1]. The systematic-review-level evidence further describes nearly 500 patients and shows how the pathogen can have devastating effects [N1-R5]. ## 7. Conclusion

In summary, listeriosis in pregnancy is rare but can have severe maternal, fetal, and neonatal consequences [N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-F2]. The evidence strongly supports high-dose intravenous ampicillin as the first-line regimen, often combined with gentamicin, and recommends switching to oral therapy after 7 days if the patient remains asymptomatic [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. Follow-up and monitoring are essential because maternal and neonatal outcomes can be severe, and early treatment may prevent infection of the fetus or newborn [N2-F2][N3-R3]. The single-center retrospective study in Xiamen provides a particularly extreme example of the disease’s catastrophic potential and highlights the importance of timely testing and prompt treatment in pregnancy [N4-F3]. Overall, the literature supports a cautious, proactive approach to clinical suspicion, diagnostic testing, treatment, and follow-up to minimize harm [N2-F2][N3-R3][N1-F1].

Study design, population, and main findings
The single-center retrospective study is a 9-year retrospective analysis of confirmed pregnancy-associated listeriosis cases in a tertiary maternal and child health hospital in Xiamen, China, from 2015 to 2023 [N4-F3]. It included 9 pregnant women and their newborns who were diagnosed with pregnancy-associated listeriosis during pregnancy or within the first 4 weeks postpartum through microbial culture of sterile sites such as whole blood, amniotic fluid, placental swab, cerebrospinal fluid, tracheal sputum, or neonatal gastric fluid [N4-F3]. The study extracted demographic information, clinical manifestations, laboratory test results, complications, and outcomes from electronic medical records [N4-F3].

Main findings highlight a very low incidence of pregnancy-associated listeriosis in this setting: 7.15/100,000 deliveries over 9 years, with sporadic cases [N4-F3]. The clinical profile was dominated by nonspecific inflammatory symptoms: fever in 88.9%, abdominal pain in 66.7%, decreased fetal movement in 66.7%, fetal tachycardia in 66.7%, and flu-like symptoms in 55.6% [N4-F3]. Laboratory findings included elevated neutrophil percentages, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin in all pregnant women [N4-F3]. Placental pathology consistently showed acute chorioamnionitis and micro-abscesses [N4-F3]. Although all pregnant women recovered, the feto-neonatal mortality rate was extremely high: 70.0% (7/10) [N4-F3]. Of the 10 offspring, only 5 survived birth and only 3 were eventually cured [N4-F3]. The study also reports antibacterial susceptibility results showing susceptibility to ampicillin, penicillin, meropenem, erythromycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole [N4-F3].

The study’s strengths include its explicit methodology: a single-center retrospective design, inclusion of sterile-site cultures, and detailed collection of demographic, clinical, laboratory, complication, and outcome data [N4-F3]. It also provides antibacterial susceptibility data on isolated Listeria monocytogenes strains [N4-F3]. However, the study has notable limitations. It is a single-center study spanning nine years but including only nine cases [N4-R1]. The small sample size limits statistical power and generalizability [N4-R1]. Another study mentioned in the search results similarly states that pregnancy-associated listeriosis is recognized as one of the worst maternal infections and notes several limitations to its study [N4-R2]. A case-series search result also notes that although the study is a retrospective study with a limited number of cases, the findings highlight the importance of vigilant surveillance of at-risk populations [N4-R3].

The study fits with the broader literature by confirming the severe consequences of listeriosis in pregnancy. The review evidence states that listeriosis in pregnancy can result in severe adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes including miscarriage, preterm labor, fetal death, and neonatal meningitis and sepsis [N1-F1]. The systematic-review-level evidence further describes nearly 500 patients and shows how the pathogen can have devastating effects [N1-R5]. Overall, the study is a clinically important, albeit limited, contribution because it demonstrates the extreme vulnerability of fetuses and newborns to listeriosis and supports the view that this infection should be treated as a high-risk condition [N4-F3].

The first-line antibiotic regimen in the evidence is high-dose intravenous ampicillin. In addition, the single-center study reports susceptibility to ampicillin, penicillin, meropenem, erythromycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole [N4-F3].

The recommended dose is high-dose intravenous ampicillin: at least 6 g/day for nonallergic patients [N2-R1]. The CDC clinical-care page recommends IV ampicillin and gentamicin for 14 to 21 days [N2-R4]. The ACOG guidance also states that IV ampicillin should be used for at least 14 days [N2-R1]. Clinical suspicion and diagnostic criteria
Clinical suspicion should be high in pregnant women who present with fever, myalgia, backache, headache, diarrhea, or other gastrointestinal symptoms [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that maternal infection may be asymptomatic, but fetal and neonatal infections can be severe [N2-F2]. The ACOG Committee Opinion explicitly states that an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and signs and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be simultaneously tested and treated [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page also emphasizes that prompt administration of antibiotics prevents infection of the fetus or newborn and that the page presents a framework for assessment and medical treatment of high-risk people, including pregnant women [N3-R3]. Diagnostic criteria include isolation of Listeria monocytogenes from a normally sterile site, such as blood or cerebrospinal fluid [N2-F2]. The single-center study uses sterile-site cultures, including whole blood, amniotic fluid, placental swab, cerebrospinal fluid, tracheal sputum, or neonatal gastric fluid [N4-F3].

Presumptive exposure management
Presumptive exposure management is more cautious than confirmed infection. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that no testing or treatment is indicated for an asymptomatic pregnant woman who reports consumption of a recalled or implicated product [N2-F2]. Similarly, a pregnant woman who ate a recalled product and is afebrile with signs and symptoms consistent with a minor gastrointestinal or flu-like illness can be managed expectantly [N2-F2]. However, an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be tested and treated simultaneously [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page also notes that outbreak-related cases have highlighted the need for guidance for known or suspected cases associated with outbreaks and product recalls [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a tiered approach: avoid testing and treatment for asymptomatic exposure, manage expectantly for mild exposure, and test and treat promptly when fever and symptoms are present [N2-F2].

Treatment and follow-up matter because listeriosis in pregnancy can have severe maternal, fetal, and neonatal consequences [N1-F1]. The review evidence states that early treatment has been shown to improve fetal and neonatal outcomes [N1-F1]. Follow-up is also important because maternal and neonatal outcomes can be severe, and early treatment may prevent infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. The CDC clinical-care page emphasizes that prompt administration of antibiotics prevents infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. When and how maternal follow-up should be performed
Maternal follow-up should be performed after confirmed or suspected listeriosis because of the risk of severe maternal and fetal/neonatal consequences [N2-F2][N3-R3]. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and signs and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be simultaneously tested and treated [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page likewise presents a framework for assessment and medical treatment of high-risk people, including pregnant women, and emphasizes prompt administration of antibiotics to prevent infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. In practice, follow-up should be guided by clinical response, symptom resolution, and the need to rule out complications.

Neonatal monitoring strategies after infection
Neonatal monitoring should be intensive after maternal listeriosis because fetal and neonatal infections can be severe. The evidence notes that neonatal infections can result in neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page recommends that pregnant women and neonates be included in the framework for assessment and medical treatment of high-risk people [N3-R3]. The single-center study includes neonatal gastric fluid cultures and reports neonatal outcomes, suggesting that neonatal surveillance should be part of the diagnostic and follow-up process [N4-F3]. Neonatal monitoring should therefore include clinical observation for signs of infection, appropriate laboratory testing, and imaging if indicated, with prompt treatment if infection is confirmed.

When to discontinue follow-up and what to document
Follow-up should be discontinued when the patient is asymptomatic and has been responding well to treatment, but evidence suggests that discontinuation should be carefully managed rather than automatic. The evidence supports switching from intravenous to oral therapy after 7 days of treatment if the patient remains asymptomatic [N2-R5]. For maternal follow-up, the ACOG guidance notes that asymptomatic exposure does not require testing or treatment, but the patient should be instructed to return if symptoms develop within 2 months [N3-R2]. For neonatal follow-up, the evidence does not provide a specific cutoff, but the broader clinical logic is that close monitoring should continue until the neonate is clinically stable and free of infection. Documentation should include the date of exposure, symptoms, treatment initiated, response to treatment, laboratory results, imaging results, and any complications observed [N2-F2][N3-R2].

Preventive follow-up after asymptomatic exposure
Preventive follow-up is indicated after asymptomatic exposure to recalled or implicated food products. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that no testing or treatment is indicated for an asymptomatic pregnant woman who reports consumption of a recalled or implicated product [N2-F2]. However, the same guidance instructs an asymptomatic patient to return if she develops symptoms of listeriosis within 2 months of eating the recalled or implicated product [N3-R2]. The evidence supports this as a way to detect early signs of infection before it becomes severe [N2-F2][N3-R2].

The evidence supports this as a way to detect early signs of infection before it becomes severe [N2-F2][N3-R2].

## 5. Diagnosis and management context

### Clinical suspicion and diagnostic criteria

Clinical suspicion should be high in pregnant women who present with fever, myalgia, backache, headache, diarrhea, or other gastrointestinal symptoms [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that maternal infection may be asymptomatic, but fetal and neonatal infections can be severe [N2-F2]. The ACOG Committee Opinion explicitly states that an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and signs and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be simultaneously tested and treated [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page also emphasizes that prompt administration of antibiotics prevents infection of the fetus or newborn and that the page presents a framework for assessment and medical treatment of high-risk people, including pregnant women [N3-R3]. Diagnostic criteria include isolation of Listeria monocytogenes from a normally sterile site, such as blood or cerebrospinal fluid [N2-F2]. The single-center study uses sterile-site cultures, including whole blood, amniotic fluid, placental swab, cerebrospinal fluid, tracheal sputum, or neonatal gastric fluid [N4-F3].

### Presumptive exposure management

Presumptive exposure management is more cautious than confirmed infection. The ACOG Committee Opinion states that no testing or treatment is indicated for an asymptomatic pregnant woman who reports consumption of a recalled or implicated product [N2-F2]. Similarly, a pregnant woman who ate a recalled product and is afebrile with signs and symptoms consistent with a minor gastrointestinal or flu-like illness can be managed expectantly [N2-F2]. However, an exposed pregnant woman with fever >38.1°C and symptoms consistent with listeriosis should be tested and treated simultaneously [N2-F2]. The CDC clinical-care page also notes that outbreak-related cases have highlighted the need for guidance for known or suspected cases associated with outbreaks and product recalls [N2-F2]. The evidence therefore supports a tiered approach: avoid testing and treatment for asymptomatic exposure, manage expectantly for mild exposure, and test and treat promptly when fever and symptoms are present [N2-F2].

### Why treatment and follow-up matter clinically

Treatment and follow-up matter because listeriosis in pregnancy can have severe maternal, fetal, and neonatal consequences [N1-F1]. The review evidence states that early treatment has been shown to improve fetal and neonatal outcomes [N1-F1]. The ACOG guidance notes that maternal infection may result in fetal loss, preterm labor, neonatal sepsis, meningitis, and death [N2-F2]. The single-center study’s extremely high feto-neonatal mortality rate of 70.0% (7/10) further underscores the clinical importance of prompt treatment [N4-F3]. Follow-up is also important because maternal and neonatal outcomes can be severe, and early treatment may prevent infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. The CDC clinical-care page emphasizes that prompt administration of antibiotics prevents infection of the fetus or newborn [N3-R3]. Therefore, both timely treatment and ongoing follow-up are essential to minimize harm [N2-F2][N3-R3].

## 6. Single-center retrospective study

### Study design, population, and main findings

The single-center retrospective study is a 9-year retrospective analysis of confirmed pregnancy-associated listeriosis cases in a tertiary maternal and child health hospital in Xiamen, China, from 2015 to 2023 [N4-F3]. It included 9 pregnant women and their newborns who were diagnosed with pregnancy-associated listeriosis during pregnancy or within the first 4 weeks postpartum through microbial culture of sterile sites such as whole blood, amniotic fluid, placental swab, cerebrospinal fluid, tracheal sputum, or neonatal gastric fluid [N4-F3]. The study extracted demographic information, clinical manifestations, laboratory test results, complications, and outcomes from electronic medical records [N4-F3].

Main findings highlight a very low incidence of pregnancy-associated listeriosis in this setting: 7.15/100,000 deliveries over 9 years, with sporadic cases [N4-F3]. The clinical profile was dominated by nonspecific inflammatory symptoms: fever in 88.9%, abdominal pain in 66.7%, decreased fetal movement in 66.7%, fetal tachycardia in 66.7%, and flu-like symptoms in 55.6% [N4-F3]. Laboratory findings included elevated neutrophil percentages, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin in all pregnant women [N4-F3]. Placental pathology consistently showed acute chorioamnionitis and micro-abscesses [N4-F3]. Although all pregnant women recovered, the feto-neonatal mortality rate was extremely high: 70.0% (7/10) [N4-F3]. Of the 10 offspring, only 5 survived birth and only 3 were eventually cured [N4-F3]. The study also reports antibacterial susceptibility results showing susceptibility to ampicillin, penicillin, meropenem, erythromycin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole [N4-F3].

### Strengths and limitations of the study

The study’s strengths include its explicit methodology: a single-center retrospective design, inclusion of sterile-site cultures, and detailed collection of demographic, clinical, laboratory, complication, and outcome data [N4-F3]. It also provides antibacterial susceptibility data on isolated Listeria monocytogenes strains [N4-F3]. However, the study has notable limitations. It is a single-center study spanning nine years but including only nine cases [N4-R1]. The small sample size limits statistical power and generalizability [N4-R1]. Another study mentioned in the search results similarly states that pregnancy-associated listeriosis is recognized as one of the worst maternal infections and notes several limitations to its study [N4-R2]. A case-series search result also notes that although the study is a retrospective study with a limited number of cases, the findings highlight the importance of vigilant surveillance of at-risk populations [N4-R3].

### How it fits with existing literature and what it adds

The study fits with the broader literature by confirming the severe consequences of listeriosis in pregnancy. The review evidence states that listeriosis in pregnancy can result in severe adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes including miscarriage, preterm labor, fetal death, and neonatal meningitis and sepsis [N1-F1]. The systematic-review-level evidence further describes nearly 500 patients and shows how the pathogen can have devastating effects [N1-R5]. In the Xiamen study, the case-fatality rate among offspring is especially extreme: 70.0% feto-neonatal mortality [N4-F3], which is far higher than the 29% perinatal mortality rate reported in a U.S. active surveillance study of 760 listeriosis cases, where 17% were pregnancy-associated [N2-F2]. The Xiamen study also adds local epidemiological detail, showing that even in a relatively low-incidence setting, the disease can have catastrophic outcomes and underscores the importance of timely testing in cases of inflammation and infection signs [N4-F3].

## 7. Conclusion

In summary, listeriosis in pregnancy is rare but can have severe maternal, fetal, and neonatal consequences [N1-F1][N1-R4][N2-F2]. The evidence strongly supports high-dose intravenous ampicillin as the first-line regimen, often combined with gentamicin, and recommends switching to oral therapy after 7 days if the patient remains asymptomatic [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. Follow-up and monitoring are essential because maternal and neonatal outcomes can be severe, and early treatment may prevent infection of the fetus or newborn [N2-F2][N3-R3]. The single-center retrospective study in Xiamen provides a particularly extreme example of the disease’s catastrophic potential and highlights the importance of timely testing and prompt treatment in pregnancy [N4-F3]. Overall, the literature supports a cautious, proactive approach to clinical suspicion, diagnostic testing, treatment, and follow-up to minimize harm [N2-F2][N3-R3][N1-F1].
